title: Why Queues Grow, Linger, and Clear

scenes.purpose: Shows a single-desk line that lengthens and later shrinks, raising the question of what drives each change.

visual.title: One Desk: The Line Grows, Then Shrinks

narration.text: Picture one desk, with one person being helped and one waiting.
More people walk up, and the line slowly grows longer.
The person at the desk finishes and heads for the exit.
The next person in line steps up to be served.
Later, nobody new arrives, and that customer finishes too.
Another person steps up, and the line is shorter now.
So what made it grow, what makes lines linger, and what clears them?

scenes.purpose: Raises the common belief that a second desk fixes a line, promises to test it, and sets the ground rules for the video.

visual.title: Does a Second Desk Fix the Line?

narration.text: Surely a second desk simply fixes a line, right?
A second desk takes the next person. Does that settle it? We will test it.
First, the rules. Everyone shares one line, first come, first served.
Newcomers join the back, and nobody leaves early or gets turned away.
On screen, movement speeds are not real service rates.

scenes.purpose: Shows one desk so the viewer can count waiting, in service, and total unfinished as a customer finishes and the next steps up.

visual.title: Who Is Waiting, Who Is Served

narration.text: With those rules set, let's count who is where at one desk.
One customer is at the desk, being served. Three more stand in line, waiting.
So waiting is three, in service is one, and the total unfinished is four.
Now the customer at the desk finishes and walks out the exit.
In service drops to zero, and the total unfinished drops to three.
Next, the person at the front of the line steps up to the desk.
Waiting drops to two and in service rises to one, but the total stays three.
Stepping up finishes nobody. Only the earlier exit lowered the total.

scenes.purpose: Explains that stepping up ends waiting time but not time in the system, which only ends with completion and departure.

visual.title: Waiting Time Versus Time in the System
visual.definition: All the time from arriving to leaving: waiting time plus time being served.
visual.example: At the desk, your wait is over, but your visit is not.

narration.text: Waiting time ends the moment service begins, but time in the system keeps running.
Time in the system covers everything from arriving to leaving, waiting plus service.
Picture yourself stepping up to the desk. Your wait is over, but your visit is not.
Only when service is complete and you walk out does the total unfinished go down.
So keep three counts in mind: waiting, in service, and the total still unfinished.

scenes.purpose: Sets up four unfinished parcels at one bench and shows two arrivals and one completion raising the total to five.

visual.title: Two In, One Out: Four Becomes Five

narration.text: Let's put those three counts to work at a packing bench.
One parcel is on the bench, and three wait behind it. That's four unfinished.
The total is the starting count, plus arrivals, minus completions.
Now two new parcels arrive and join the back of the line.
The parcel on the bench is finished, and it leaves for good.
The next parcel moves onto the bench. Waiting drops, but it's still unfinished.
Now one is on the bench and four wait. Four plus two minus one is five.

scenes.purpose: Shows one arrival and two completions bringing the total from five down to four.

visual.title: One In, Two Out: Five Becomes Four

narration.text: Next round begins with those five unfinished parcels.
This time, only one new parcel arrives at the line.
Meanwhile, the parcel on the bench is completed and heads out.
The next waiting parcel moves up, and packing begins.
It's packed, then it leaves too. That's two completions so far.
Another waiting parcel moves up onto the empty bench.
Five plus one minus two leaves four. More completions than arrivals shrink the work.

scenes.purpose: Shows one arrival matched by one completion so the total stays at four, holding the backlog in place.

visual.title: One In, One Out: Still Four

narration.text: Last round starts at four: one on the bench, three waiting.
One new parcel arrives and joins the back of the line.
Then the parcel on the bench finishes and leaves the room.
The next parcel moves onto the bench to be packed.
Still one on the bench, three waiting, and four unfinished.
Matching counts hold the backlog steady. They don't make it disappear.

scenes.purpose: Shows how a burst of arrivals and one long job build and hold a line at a single unchanged server.

visual.title: A burst arrives at a busy server

narration.text: Now let's see what timing does, with packets at a single server.
This server handles one packet at a time, and it's busy now.
Then three packets arrive almost together, one right after another.
With the server busy, they form a waiting line of three.
The first packet finishes and leaves, freeing the server for the next.
The next packet starts, but it needs much more work than usual.
It stays at the server a long time, so the two behind it linger.

scenes.purpose: Shows a quiet spell with no arrivals letting the same server empty the line, and why one snapshot or average misses this.

visual.title: A quiet spell lets the server catch up

narration.text: Now no new packets arrive. This quiet spell lets the server catch up.
At last, the packet needing extra work finishes and leaves.
The next packet moves up from the line and starts.
This one is quick, so it finishes and leaves soon after.
The last packet starts, and the waiting line is now empty.
Moments later it finishes too, and the server sits idle.
The server never changed. A burst built the line; a quiet spell cleared it.
A snapshot or average misses this: three waiting at one moment, none at another.

scenes.purpose: Shows that opening a second desk moves a waiting person into service without changing the unfinished total.

narration.text: Now, instead of timing, we change the service side.
One desk is busy and four people wait, so five are unfinished in total.
Now a second desk opens, and the person at the front steps straight up to it.
Three wait and two are served. The total stays five, since nobody has finished yet.

scenes.purpose: Demonstrates that with two desks, three arrivals and two completions still grow the total, just more slowly than with one desk.

narration.text: Now three people will arrive while each desk completes one customer.
A newcomer joins the back of the line while both desks keep working.
Busy desks are not departures yet.
Each desk finishes its customer, and both walk out the exit.
The next two step up, because a desk needs someone to serve.
Two more people arrive, making three arrivals against two departures.
The total rose from five to six. One desk finishing only one customer would have made it seven.
So the second desk slowed the growth, but the backlog did not shrink.

scenes.purpose: Shows a later interval where two desks complete more than arrive, so the total falls, separating helping from clearing.

narration.text: Later, arrivals ease off while the two desks keep working.
Both desks finish, and two customers leave through the exit.
Each desk takes the next person from the front of the line.
Only one new person arrives during this stretch.
Then both desks finish again, and two more customers head out.
The next two step up. Four left and one arrived, so six fell to three.
Capacity helps, but only completions outpacing arrivals shrink a backlog.

scenes.purpose: Shows the three counts again and how arrivals and completions grow or hold the unfinished total at a single desk.

narration.text: Let's recap with counts: two wait, one is served, three are unfinished.
Only a completion removes someone from the total, like this customer leaving now.
Stepping up shrinks the waiting line, but that person is still unfinished.
Two newcomers arrive after one completion, so the backlog grows from three to four.
Next, one customer finishes and leaves, dropping the total to three.
One arrival matches that one completion, so the total is back at four.
The next person steps up; waiting shrinks, but four remain unfinished.

scenes.purpose: Recalls how bursts form temporary lines, what a second desk changes, and how more completions than arrivals clear the line, ending with a recap.

visual.title: Bursts, Quiet Spells, and a Second Desk

narration.text: Now picture two desks, each helping one customer, with nobody waiting.
A burst of arrivals, or a few slow jobs, can build a temporary line.
Both desks finish at the same time, and two customers head out.
With a second desk, two waiting people start sooner, shortening their waits.
Extra capacity can slow a backlog's growth, but clearing needs more completions than arrivals.
In a quiet spell, both desks finish while nobody new arrives, and the system empties.
Count arrivals and completions, and you can tell whether a line grows, lingers, or clears.
